title: Ξύλα καὶ ἐλαία
part: The Trees and the Olive (Chambry 252 · Perry 262)
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 252 (= Perry 262). Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« », ⟨ ⟩ for editorial supplements). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Ξύλα ποτὲ ἐπορεύθη τοῦ χειροτονῆσαι ἐφ’ ἑαυτῶν βασιλέα καὶ εἶπαν τῇ ἐλαίᾳ· « Βασίλευσον ἐφ’ ἡμῶν. »
sentences.tr: Xyla pote eporeuthē tou cheirotonēsai eph’ heautōn basilea kai eipan tēi elaiāi· « Basileuson eph’ hēmōn. »
sentences.l: The trees once went to elect a king over themselves, and they said to the olive: « Be king over us. »
sentences.n: This is Jotham's fable from the ninth chapter of Judges, standing here among the Aesopic fables in Greek of the Septuagint's kind, though not word for word the Septuagint's: here the trees go to elect (χειροτονῆσαι) where Judges has them go to anoint, and the vine, which in Judges is asked between the fig and the bramble, is passed over. The Greek keeps the marks of translation: εἶπαν for εἶπον, and τοῦ χειροτονῆσαι, a genitive articular infinitive of purpose. ξύλον is 'wood, timber' and in this Greek simply 'tree'. ἐπί with the genitive of persons is 'over' them, of rule.

sentences.t: Καὶ εἶπεν αὐτοῖς ἡ ἐλαία· « Ἀφεῖσα τὴν πιότητά μου ἣν ἐδόξασεν ἐν ἐμοὶ ὁ θεὸς καὶ οἱ ἄνθρωποι, πορευθῶ ἄρχειν τῶν ξύλων ; »
sentences.tr: Kai eipen autois hē elaia· « Apheisa tēn piotēta mou hēn edoxasen en emoi ho theos kai hoi anthrōpoi, poreuthō archein tōn xylōn ; »
sentences.l: And the olive said to them: « Having given up my fatness, which God and men have glorified in me, am I to go to rule over the trees? »
sentences.i: And the olive said to them: « Am I to leave behind the richness that God and men have honoured in me, and go to rule the trees? »
sentences.n: πιότης is fatness, and in an olive that means the oil — the whole of its worth. πορευθῶ is a deliberative subjunctive, the question a speaker puts to himself: 'am I to go?'. The space before the Greek question mark is Chambry's French printing house and is kept as part of his page. ὁ θεός is capitalized as 'God' here, against this collection's usual 'the god', because the speaker is the God of Judges and not one of the Olympians.

sentences.t: Καὶ εἶπαν τὰ ξύλα τῇ συκῇ· « Δεῦρο, βασίλευσον ἐφ’ ἡμῶν. »
sentences.tr: Kai eipan ta xyla tēi sykēi· « Deuro, basileuson eph’ hēmōn. »
sentences.l: And the trees said to the fig: « Come, be king over us. »
sentences.n: δεῦρο is properly 'hither', used as a summons: 'come here, come on'.

sentences.t: Καὶ εἶπεν αὐτὴ ἡ συκῆ· « Ἀφεῖσα τὴν γλυκύτητά μου καὶ τὸ γέννημά μου τὸ ἀγαθόν, πορευθῶ τοῦ ἄρχειν τῶν ξύλων ; »
sentences.tr: Kai eipen autē hē sykē· « Apheisa tēn glykytēta mou kai to gennēma mou to agathon, poreuthō tou archein tōn xylōn ; »
sentences.l: And the fig herself said: « Having given up my sweetness and my good fruit, am I to go to rule over the trees? »
sentences.i: And the fig said: « Am I to leave behind my sweetness and my good fruit, and go to rule the trees? »
sentences.n: γέννημα is what a plant brings forth, its produce. The fig answers in the olive's words but with τοῦ ἄρχειν where the olive had a plain ἄρχειν — the same articular infinitive of purpose as in the opening line, and Chambry prints the two differently.

sentences.t: Καὶ εἶπαν τὰ ξύλα πρὸς τὴν ῥάμνον· « Δεῦρο, βασίλευσον ἐφ’ ἡμῶν. »
sentences.tr: Kai eipan ta xyla pros tēn rhamnon· « Deuro, basileuson eph’ hēmōn. »
sentences.l: And the trees said to the buckthorn: « Come, be king over us. »
sentences.n: ῥάμνος is a low thorn bush of no use for timber or fruit; the trees have worked their way down from the most valuable to the least.

sentences.t: Καὶ εἶπεν ἡ ῥάμνος ⟨πρὸς⟩ τὰ ξύλα· « Εἰ ἐν ἀληθείᾳ ὑμεῖς χρίετέ με εἰς βασιλέα ἐφ’ ὑμῶν, δεῦτε ὑπόστητε ἐν τῇ σκέπῃ μου· καὶ εἰ μή, ἐξέλθοι πῦρ ἐκ τῆς ῥάμνου καὶ καταφάγοι τὰς κέδρους τοῦ Λιβάνου. »
sentences.tr: Kai eipen hē rhamnos ⟨pros⟩ ta xyla· « Ei en alētheiāi hymeis chriete me eis basilea eph’ hymōn, deute hypostēte en tēi skepēi mou· kai ei mē, exelthoi pyr ek tēs rhamnou kai kataphagoi tas kedrous tou Libanou. »
sentences.l: And the buckthorn said ⟨to⟩ the trees: « If in truth you are anointing me as king over you, come, take your stand under my shelter; and if not, let fire come out from the buckthorn and devour the cedars of Lebanon. »
sentences.i: And the buckthorn said to the trees: « If you are truly anointing me king over you, then come and shelter beneath me; and if not, let fire come out of the buckthorn and devour the cedars of Lebanon. »
sentences.n: ⟨πρός⟩ is Chambry's own supplement, his angle brackets marking a word he adds. χρίω εἰς βασιλέα, 'anoint as king', is the Septuagint's idiom for making a king. ἐξέλθοι and καταφάγοι are optatives of wish — a curse laid down, not a prediction. The threat is empty and enormous at once: a thorn bush casts a shade that shelters nothing, and the cedars of Lebanon were the tallest and costliest timber known. Chambry prints no moral for this fable, and none is supplied here.
